s: Monks follow Mahâvîra’s austerities, renouncing wishes and plans. They cease from sin, guard themselves, avoid violence and attachment, bear pain, wander homeless, and assure safety to all beings. Living on pure water and abstaining from ablutions, they eat for control, subdue passions, seek liberation, and annihilate Karman through endurance and control.

Akriyâvâdins is a heretical creed among doctrines: it denies Karman and transmission of the soul’s action to future moments. Its contradictory adherents fail to understand truth, are countered by a valiant opinion, and may cause rebirth in the Circle of Births.

is_a passion [defiles the soul] A wise man should conquer greed after considering the impermanence of good places and the limited duration of relations and friendships. The pious man is instructed to remain free from greed.
Earth, foundation of all things, contains life; fire burns beings in earth and dirt-born vermin.
Water contains life and houses many beings; contact brings no perfection, use can kill beings, and it does not wash off sin.
is_killed_by men [when extinguished] Lighting a fire kills living beings, while extinguishing it kills the fire. Fire-tending is not a means of attaining perfection.

Men are living beings who harm their souls and become wicked by hurting, killing, burning, or destroying beings and seeds for pleasure; they are born again as such beings, then die when their lives expire.

A wise man understands that living beings desire happiness and therefore follows the Law through carefulness, nonviolence, wisdom, and restraint from pleasures. He conquers greed and sins, enters the noble path, and uses meditation to cover past wrongdoing while withdrawing from harmful action, senses, Karman, and language. As life approaches its end, he learns a religious death. By avoiding new acts and understanding the world’s sins, wise men pass beyond misery, reach excellence, or become liberated.

Sin is committed through harming living beings, destroying seeds, pleasure in fire, careless conduct, violence, false speech, attachment, and assenting to others’ injury. Its causes include deceit, greed, anger, and pride. It increases Karman and brings misery, wailing, suffering, trembling, and misery on decease; wisdom requires abstaining from its causes.
Violence toward movable and immovable beings is condemned. A wise monk should abstain from violence and give assurance of safety to all beings.

Liberation is the real, best, distant goal of religious practice and virtuous exertion. It is freedom from Samsâra, reached when Karman is annihilated and one does not return to the world. It is wrongly linked to bathing, water, fire, and other outward practices. A monk seeks it through meditation, religious practices, carefulness, right knowledge and conduct, renunciation of pride, deceit, sin, attachment, worldly vanities, and causes of worldly existence. It requires realizing singleness and solitude, and is not gained by a monk who still acts like a householder. It is finally obtained through the highest good, austerities, silence, and pure food.

l: Eighth Lecture, Called on Exertion, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: is_a lecture The Eighth Lecture, Called on Exertion, explains two definitions of exertion and distinguishes exertion leading to works from exertion not leading to works.
Exertion has two forms: sinners pursue works, while wise men abstain from works and the virtuous strive toward distant liberation.
practise abstention from works The virtuous exert themselves toward liberation, live indifferent to their own happiness, remain calm, and avoid attachment.

Works, linked to carelessness and sinful thoughts, words, and acts, are attributed to sinners through exertion. They bring misery, worldly bondage, and suffering, especially when they cause living beings’ death; a wise man avoids injuring living beings.
Carelessness is identified as the cause of Karman, unfolding through sins in thought, word, and act by oneself or others.

is_taught monk [as the proper mode of wandering] Carefulness requires avoiding injury, unallowed food, false speech, worldly attachment, and actions that cause guilt. It includes guarding speech, restraining the senses, enduring troubles, and remaining impartial.
A person following the right doctrine exerts himself. A houseless monk who knows the pith of the Law by intuition or instruction should follow it and abstain from sins.

The noble path, preached by Mahâvîra, contains all virtues and is not blamed. After conquering greed, a wise man enters this difficult route across Samsâra through study, non-injury, restraint, proper alms, and abandoning passions, leading to liberation from misery.
Right faith opposes heretical teachings and talk, and is associated with good exertion without evil consequences.
A monk should use as few words as possible, avoid deceiving speech and delight in another's foibles, reflect before answering, keep secrets, and avoid forbidden or vulgar forms of address.

Conduct requires restraint from harmful acts, worldly interests, improper associations, and indulgence. A virtuous monk should remain controlled, endure suffering, and avoid company that brings disguised dangers.
A restrained and learned monk should accept only what is freely given, remaining circumspect about accepting alms and abstaining from what he is forbidden to accept.

l: Ninth Lecture, Called the Law, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: is_a lecture [ninth in sequence] The Ninth Lecture, Called the Law, teaches the Law preached by Mahâvîra, the duties and restraints of a monk, and the path toward final Liberation.

l: Tenth Lecture, Called Carefulness, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: A lecture teaching monks seeking Liberation carefulness, restraint, non-injury, truth, and freedom from worldly ties.
Arhat, a wise person, pondered on the Law and proclaimed its teaching on carefulness.
Worldly ties include attachment to women, property, wealth, cattle, relations, dear friends, honours, and fame. A sage should wander free from all such ties.

is_escaped_by wise men [through knowledge of the world's sins and avoidance of new acts] Misery is overcome by a purified soul compared to a ship reaching the shore. Those who destroy their former works and undertake no new acts get beyond misery.

A Leader, Saviour, and Venerable One who knows past, present, and future, removes obstacles to right faith, and incomparably knows and expounds the Law. Not inclined to heretical doctrines, he affirms his teaching as true and explains the names Brâhmana, Sramana, Bhikshu, and Nirgrantha.
A man studies six classes of living beings, refrains from killing, restrains his senses, treats creatures as himself, abandons pride and deceit, and correctly enters the Path to cross Samsâra.

l: six classes of living beings, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: includes living beings [six classes] The six classes are earth-lives, water-lives, fire-lives, wind-lives, grass, trees, and corn, together with the remaining movable beings as enumerated in the text. They comprise all living beings, with no others besides.
The senses are subdued by the person who is called a Brâhmana, Sramana, Bhikshu, or Nirgrantha.

involves slaughter of living beings [when beings are killed for its sake] When food and drink are prepared as a gift, praising the gift makes one accessory to the killing of beings, while forbidding it deprives others of their means of subsistence. Giving neither judgment avoids guilt.

l: slaughter of living beings, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: Slaughter of living beings may occur in preparing a gift of food and drink. A monk must not accept food specially prepared with such slaughter or assent to anyone killing beings.

The Tîrthakaras proclaim Law as a place of safety for beings suffering in Samsâra, serve as the world’s eyes and leaders, teach a salutary path to men, and declare the world eternal because creatures live in it.
have_as_foundation Peace [past and future Buddhas] The Buddhas that were and the Buddhas that will be have Peace as their foundation, just as all things have the earth for their foundation.

is_a foundation [of the Buddhas that were and will be] Peace is the foundation of the Buddhas and the condition associated with Nirvâna. One who has gained this foundation is not overpowered by accidents, as a mountain is not overpowered by a storm.

l: Twelfth Lecture, Called the Creed, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: is_a lecture It presents four creeds and contrasts their teachings concerning truth, action, Karman, the world, misery, and liberation.
Heretical creed upheld by various Vinaya adherents, claiming Môksha through Vinaya; its upholders mistake truth and goodness, explaining their tenet without perceiving truth.
A group claiming cleverness reasons incoherently, remains confused, and includes ignorant teachers who unreflectively teach untruth to ignorant pupils.

l: right knowledge and conduct, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: lead_to liberation They lead to liberation.

l: birth and death, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: are_known_by one entitled to expound the Kriyâvâda They are among the matters known by the man who understands himself, the world, and the future existences of men.

l: Thirteenth Lecture, Called the Real Truth, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: is_a lecture The Thirteenth Lecture, Called the Real Truth, expounds the qualities of men, the virtue and peace of the good, and the vices and unrest of the wicked. It teaches conduct, humility, self-control, truthful instruction, and release from the Circle of Births.

Men are taught the Law and instructed in conduct, yet may neglect it through rude speech, false explanations, untruth, concealment, quarrelsomeness, deceit, pride, and attachment to sensual objects. They are urged instead to control themselves, obey their teacher, and conform impartially to admonitions, becoming beyond deceit. False conduct and seeking honour through knowledge, birth, or austerities bring harm or continued rebirth.

Tathâgatas teach the Law through diligent teachers. Wise, supreme, and the eyes of the world, they engage in no undertakings; therefore the text asks how they could be born again and states that they are not born again.
A teacher guides a monk by exemplary conduct and instruction, enabling performance of duties, learning the Law, and ending mundane existence.
Gôtra, within Gaina church’s Vow of Silence, does not make a person virtuous or capable of final progress; great sages rise above it to no Gôtra.
A novice, initially unversed in Law and belonging to Gakkha, may be led away by unprincipled men, but through the Ginas’ words comes to know the Law well.

Creed is a pure, complete, unparalleled law in accordance with Ginas that surpasses the world. It must be faithfully followed and taught without distortion; requiring non-hostility and renunciation, it affects creatures differently and may lead men to perfected sainthood or godhood.

gives bright ideas [when heard by a monk] The Truth is heard, understood, and taught through pure speech consistent with the creed. A monk should explain it at suitable length without distortion or needless difficulty.

l: Fifteenth Lecture, Called the Yamakas, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: A lecture called Yamakas teaches the Law, control, Karman, misery, Môksha, and beings from men to Tathâgatas.
The Great Hero is a being without Karman who understands Karman, is not born again or dies, annihilates former works, and creates no new works.
Men who are not seduced by women value Môksha, become free from bondage, do not desire life, and in the human world can fulfil the Law and become perfected saints or gods.

l: Sixteenth Lecture, Called the Song, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: It explains why a person who subdues the senses, is well qualified, and abandons the body is called a Brâhmana, Sramana, Bhikshu, or Nirgrantha.
A religious ascetic ceases sinful actions, possesses Samitis, exerts himself without anger or pride, subdues senses, and abandons body.

A Bhikshu is a modest religious ascetic obedient to the Guru, sustaining troubles and calamities, practising prescribed conduct with a pure mind, exerting himself steadfastly, eating moderately from others, subduing senses, and abandoning body.

A Nirgrantha is a religious ascetic: single, awakened, disciplined, and knowing the absolute âtman and true Self. Possessing Samitis and equanimity, it renounces sin and worldly honour, seeks and knows the Law, subdues senses, strives for Liberation, and abandons the body.

Sutrakritanga, Book II begins with Sudharman recounting Mahâvîra’s teachings. The First Lecture, “the Lotus,” uses a lotus-pool simile to explain the world, Karman, pleasure, teachers, the Law, preaching, and Nirvâna, then rejects doctrines identifying soul with body or making elements, Self, or Fate the sole cause of everything. It urges renunciation, nonviolence, mendicancy, chastity, and freedom from possessions and passions, stressing that neither wealth, relations, nor the body protects against suffering and death. The following lectures distinguish sinful, meritorious, and mixed activity: violence, lying, theft, pride, deceit, greed, harmful occupations, and occult practices bring bad Karman, hell, and Samsâra, while careful monks destroy Karman and attain Kêvala, liberation, Nirvâna, and final beatitude. The text repeatedly teaches that all beings fear pain and must not be harmed. It examines beings’ births, bodies, food, growth, and Karman, calling for care concerning food; explains that sin can arise through mental, verbal, and bodily activity even without deliberate reflection; and presents controlled conduct as renunciation of activity. A monk is instructed to reject error, affirm the teachings of the Ginas, and seek final liberation. Ârdraka defends Mahâvîra against Gôsâla, a Buddhist, a Vêdic Priest, a Vêdântin, and a Hastitâpasa, emphasizing individual souls, compassion, avoidance of new Karman, and Kêvala knowledge. Finally, Gautama debates Udaka at Nâlandâ about vows against injury and rebirth through Karman. Udaka accepts Gautama’s view and joins Mahâvîra’s creed of five great vows and Pratikramana.

is_a scriptural discourse Sutrakritanga, Book II, First Lecture, Called the Lotus, contains Sudharman’s account of a discourse from Mahâvîra and Mahâvîra’s explanation of the lotus simile and four doctrines.
contains First Lecture, Called the Lotus Book II contains the First Lecture, Called the Lotus.

l: First Lecture, Called the Lotus, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: is_called the Lotus The First Lecture, Called the Lotus, presents a lotus-pool simile and explains its meaning through teachings about the world, conduct, doctrines, and Nirvâna.
Sudharman, a speaker, says he heard discourses from Mahâvîra and recounts them to Gambûsvâmin, including the Lotus and Knowledge of Food lectures.

Mahâvîra is a Venerable Ascetic, Sramana, and teacher, also called Gñâtriputra. He gives the lotus-pool simile and explains it to Sramanas, discusses four doctrines of heretical teachers, and teaches discourses on Activity, Knowledge of Food, and renunciation. His teaching describes acquiring Karman, sins connected with mind, speech, and body, the six classes of living beings, and the controlled monk’s avoidance and renunciation of sins. Though single and alone amid many followers, he moves from wandering as one monk to teaching many monks. He avoids wrong opinions, acquires no new Karman, annihilates old Karman, and teaches the vow leading to Môksha. At Nâlandâ, he receives Udaka into the creed of five great vows and Pratikramana.

Sramanas are long-lived religious practitioners whose true character is defined by disciplined, nonviolent conduct. They teach the Law, the great vows, and the five small vows; understand the Âsravas and their stoppage; exercise self-control; avoid Karman; and use patient, resigned, virtuous speech. They should avoid specially prepared food from compassion and fear of injuring living beings, and are not householders who use cold water, eat seeds, or have intercourse with women. The records also warn that some Sramanas kill living beings or acquire property and may relapse into such habits after becoming monks. They may be robbed, insulted, or denied alms. In the Lotus lecture, they hear a simile, ask Mahâvîra for its meaning, and receive doctrinal teaching. The account contrasts teachers of violence, destined for suffering, with those who reject violence.

l: Nirgrantha monks and nuns, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: Nirgrantha monks and nuns worship and praise Mahâvîra, then admit they do not comprehend a simile.
A water- and mud-filled lotus-pool holds many splendid white lotuses, including a large central one; four men enter and become stuck in mud while a monk remains at its bank.

are the best of Nymphaeas [tall, brilliant, of fine colour, smell, taste, and touch] The white lotuses are the best of Nymphaeas and grow throughout the lotus-pool. They are described as tall, brilliant, and splendid, and they represent people in general.

l: one big white lotus, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: The one big white lotus, the best of Nymphaeas, grows in the lotus-pool’s middle as the king; called from the bank, it flies up as Nirvâna.

A knowing, clever first man enters a lotus-pool from the Eastern quarter to fetch a big white lotus, becomes stuck in middle mud unable to reach either bank, and represents the doctrine that soul and body are identical.

A knowing, clever man from the Southern quarter sees the first man stuck in a lotus-pool, judges him unknowing, enters himself, becomes stuck, and represents the doctrine that everything consists of five elements.
The monk, living on low food and desiring to reach the shore of Samsâra, knows the way, remains on the lotus-pool bank, and raises his voice to preach the Law and call the white lotus upward.
The world exists and is represented by a lotus-pool, where men are born into differing conditions and social positions according to merit.

Karman is portrayed as a binding force, represented by water in a lotus-pool, that is acquired through activity and comes into contact with the soul. It brings beings into existence, determines their form and duration of life, actuates and changes them, and helps determine whether they are movable or immovable. Sinful actions acquire Karman that generally bears beings downward into hell, while residual good Karman can lead meritorious beings among the gods. Beings continue wandering through sentient and senseless bodies when they fail to shake off, annihilate, or destroy it. Yet Karman exists with effects that can be experienced and annihilated; bondage occurs through it. Monks seek its annihilation by avoiding killing, acquisition, sinful actions, improper food, passions, and wrong opinions. Careful religious activity allows it to arise and be destroyed across three moments, while Mahâvîra acquires no new Karman and annihilates old Karman. Avoiding it is part of the blessed life of Sramanas.

l: pleasures and amusements, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: Pleasures and amusements are represented by mud and include sounds, colours, smells, tastes, and feelings of touch. Men become stuck in them, unable to return to worldly life or get beyond them. They cannot help or save from illness or suffering; the wise consider them alien and give them up.
A strong man governing a kingdom, represented by one big white lotus, suppresses riots and mutinies and has an assembly of Ugras and sons of Ugras.
Heretical teachers, represented by four men, teach doctrines criticized by Mahâvîra and cannot free themselves or others from the Circle of Births.

The Law, represented by a monk in a simile, teaches nonviolence toward all living beings alongside abstention from cardinal sins, control, purity, simplicity, humility, freedom from bonds, cessation of passion, Nirvâna, and indifference. Searched, known, taught, explained, and praised by monks for annihilating Karman, it is constant, permanent, eternal, and true. It instructs householders and leads those who exert themselves well to final beatitude.

Nirvâna is a goal of the religious path, associated with perfection, liberation, and final delivery. It is represented by a white lotus flying up after a monk calls to it. A monk should preach it with qualities supporting peace of mind, and it is not reached through unworthy conduct.

The soul is debated: one doctrine identifies it with the body, while Nâstikas deny a separate soul; opponents cannot show or describe one apart from the body. It acquires merit at rest and experiences disturbance when demerit is present.

Âtman, identical with Soul in the first doctrine, is an entity capable of activity within the skin’s surface and lasting only as long as the body. It may remain uncontrolled and unresigned, fail to renounce activity, adhere to errors and ignorance, commit sin, and not avoid or renounce harm toward six classes of living beings.
The body, treated by the first doctrine as identical with the soul and life’s limit, includes hands, grows old, and cannot be separated from the soul.

l: first doctrine: soul and body are identical, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: asserts soul and body are one [the soul does not outlast the destruction of the body] The first doctrine teaches that soul and body are one, that life ends with the body, and that no soul exists separately from it. Its adherents are described as engaging in pleasures and amusements and failing to enter the noble path.

The Nâstikas deny a soul distinct from the body and any world beyond, saying life ends here. They pursue pleasures, remain bound in the Circle of Births, and cannot account for the moral quality or outcomes of actions, including perfection or hell.

l: second doctrine: everything consists of the five elements, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: asserts everything consists of the five elements [down to a blade of grass] The second doctrine teaches that everything, down to a blade of grass, consists of five eternal elements. Its adherents say that killing and other actions do not constitute wrongdoing and are said to remain stuck in pleasures and amusements.
The five elements, earth, water, fire, wind, and air, are uncreated, beginningless, endless, and eternal; together they constitute all living beings, all things, and the whole world.

l: third doctrine: the Self is the cause of everything, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: The third doctrine asserts that the Self causes, produces, manifests, and binds all things. Its adherents reject the twelve Aṅgas as false and remain trapped in misery, pleasures, and amusements.

l: fourth doctrine: Fate is the cause of everything, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: The fourth doctrine asserts that Fate causes everything: bodily existence, life’s changes, death, rebirth, pleasure, and pain. It denies action and personal causation, leaving adherents absorbed in pleasures and amusements.

causes pleasure and pain [according to the fourth doctrine] Fate is presented by the fourth doctrine as the cause of everything experienced by movable and immovable beings, including embodiment, life’s changes, loss of the body, states of existence, pleasure, and pain.

The twelve Aṅgas are the Canon of the Ganins, taught, produced, and declared by Sramanas and Nirgranthas; spanning Âkârâṅga through Drishtivâda, adherents of the third doctrine declare them false and untrue.

Men are people found in the East, West, North, and South, including Âryas, non-Âryas, and barbarians. They may own houses, fields, servants, and peasants, or renounce possessions and lead a mendicant's life. They are born in Karmabhûmi, Akarmabhûmi, or minor continents; cruel, proud men accompanied only by Karman are born in hell while causing others to suffer and die. Men may commit sins through motives, accident, error, lying, theft, passions, pride, mistreatment, deceit, and greed; some practise occult sciences or become agents of harm. Their degree of cessation from sin places them in demerit, merit, or a mixed state, determining suffering in hell and Samsâra, liberation, or rebirth as gods. Human beings arise in a womb and progress from parental substances to milk and solid foods.

Householders are men in a demeritorious condition with great desires, undertakings, and possessions; across East, West, North, and South, they kill living beings or acquire property directly, through others, or by consent, from love and hatred.

Brâhmanas are depicted both as acquirers of property and, in some cases, killers of living beings. They may retain or relapse into such habits after becoming monks. They can be robbed, insulted, or refused alms and should understand the thirteen kinds of committing sins. Those teaching violence face suffering and wandering in Samsâra; those teaching nonviolence avoid these consequences.

A monk is a non-killer who renounces possessions, relations, pleasures, worldly work, and household life. He lives chastely through non-killing and non-acquisition, avoids love, hatred, passions, wrong belief, and the five cardinal sins, and refuses improperly obtained food and material gain from teaching. Controlled, restrained, careful, wise, calm, and happy, he possesses Samitis, preaches the Law solely to annihilate Karman, and seeks Liberation.

Gautama stays in park Hastiyâma and debates Udaka, the son of Pêdhâla, over renunciation and injury to living beings. He rejects Udaka’s limiting interpretation, teaches that injury to movable beings is sinful, persuades Udaka, and is taken to the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra.

l: Arhats and Bhagavats, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: The Arhats and Bhagavats of the past, present, and future declare that all sorts of living beings should not be slain, treated with violence, abused, tormented, or driven away.

Living beings are one of six classes and include beings with life, divided into movable and immovable forms existing above, below, and on earth. They feel pain when ill-treated, injured by slaughter, or involved in sin, and are universally averse to pain. Therefore they should not be beaten, treated violently, abused, tormented, injured, or slain. They arise or come forth in earth and occur in earth, water, plants, animals, and other bodies. They feed on various nourishing substances, including bodies of earth, water, fire, wind, plants, and movable and immovable beings. Throughout existence they undergo changes through Karman, are impelled by Karman, and belong to the Circle of Births, where they may take different forms. The unit moves from their division and capacity for pain to food, harm, renunciation of wicked deeds, and abstention from injury against all living beings.

Relations include family, servants, friends, companions, and acquaintances across all directions; yet none can experience another person’s illness or pain, so relationship bonds cannot help or save an individual.

is_individual individual experience [each person dies individually] Each person dies individually, and no one can experience what another person has done or take upon himself another person's pains. Living beings experience pain and agony from death and other forms of ill-treatment.

The unit describes beings born in earth, water, trees, creepers, grass, herbs, plants, animals, human beings, parasites, and other bodies. Birth and origin are repeatedly connected with Karman, and beings may arise from bodies of the same or different kinds.

l: renunciation of activity, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: Renunciation of activity is a mendicant monk’s rejection of possessions, relations, pleasures, occupations, household life, and especially sinful harm to living beings. It unfolds through giving these up and becoming inactive, careful, controlled, restrained, and thoroughly wise.

is_a life of renunciation People from various families, including those with or without kinsmen and property, may renounce them and lead a mendicant's life. A monk leads this life while practising control and knowing that things are divided into living beings and things without life.

A monk should be free from wrath, pride, deceit, greed, love, hate, quarrel, calumny, reviling, and delight in sensual things. Such freedom helps him cease acquiring gross Karman and abstain from sins. The passions include anger, pride, deceit, and greed. A monk who avoids these passions is calm and happy and is regarded as controlled and restrained.

Food includes substances on which living beings feed. It should be approached carefully because of living beings involved, and a monk should consume only food that is lawfully given, pure, free from living matter, properly measured, and sufficient to sustain control and life.

Sin arises through killing or injuring living beings, slaughter, pleasure-seeking, passions, harmful conduct and speech, and food prepared through killing. It can be incurred even without sinful thoughts, speech, bodily functions, conscious consideration, or dreams. A monk avoids and renounces harm, love, and hatred, while those denying guilt for such acts are condemned as teaching and believing in error.

A monk relies on chastity as part of his religious practice and does not seek sensual pleasures or worldly rewards through it. Chastity is among the practices by which he may pursue his religious goal.

A monk should exert himself in control, abstain from sins, and consume only enough food to practise control and carry its burden. The Law is preached to those who exert themselves well and to those who do not.

Violence includes beating, abusing, tormenting, threatening, burning, depriving of life, and driving away living beings. The Law teaches that all sorts of living beings should not be treated with violence.

Liberation is an existent state, shore of Samsâra, and goal of the religious path. A monk seeks, knows, and strives to gain it by renouncing actions, worldly occupations, and householder life. It cannot be reached through suffering, killing, evil deeds, or condemned religious and worldly activity.

Final beatitude is a goal of the religious path and the ultimate destination for a wandering monk. It is reached by monks after attaining Kêvala, ending misery and completely ceasing from sin. Those instructed in the Law who cultivate virtues, abstain from sins and passions, and conduct themselves well reach it. Unworthy, impure, unholy, or sinful conduct does not lead to final delivery; the monk should improve his chances and wander until reaching liberation.

Samsâra is a beginningless, endless fourfold cycle and wilderness of wandering through birth, death, conception, regeneration, and varied existence. Violence and sin prolong wandering; perfected beings escape. A monk seeking its shore fulfils general and particular virtues while pursuing release.
Wrong belief is included among the sins associated with uncontrolled conduct and the passions. A monk abstains from the sin of wrong belief.

l: six classes of living beings, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: The six classes of living beings include earth-bodies and movable beings; seeking wants through them leads a person toward sin without renunciation.

l: immovable living beings, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: Immovable living beings include trees, creepers, grass, herbs, plants, and other bodies where living beings arise and grow. Their bodies and humours feed other living beings. Their character is shaped by Karman; killing or injury is sinful and covered by complete renunciation. After life ends, they take a new form, movable or immovable.

Merit is explained as belonging to men who practise righteousness and abstain from sinful actions; complete restraint leads monks to final beatitude directly or, through residual good Karman, to birth as gods.

Demerit is bad Karman present in men through sinning. Explained through harmful activities and thirteen kinds of committing sins, it involves unworthy, impure, unholy conduct. It belongs to those practising unrighteousness, violence, sensual indulgence, and other sinful actions, causing hell and continued wandering through Samsâra.

Bad Karman is what accrues from sinful and harmful conduct. It arises through violence, slaying, accidents, mistaken sight, lying, taking what is not freely given, mental wrath, pride, bad treatment of friends, deceit, greed, and acts done for oneself or associates. It can also accrue without personal interest, through violent occupations, and through actions against householders, Sramanas, Brâhmanas, animals, and property. The records move from particular motives and errors to a general account of harmful activity.
Hell is a dark, impure, rugged destination for men full of demerit, where after death they suffer horrid pains without sleep, consolation, comfort, recreation, or encouragement.
Gods inhabit regions as dwelling places and exist in the world; meritorious monks and Sramana followers are born as beautiful, powerful, happy gods through residual good Karman.

l: thirteen kinds of committing sins, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: The thirteen kinds of committing sins are activities practised by sentient beings, spanning interest-driven, accidental, mistaken, harmful, deceptive, greedy, and religious-life-related conduct that pious Sramanas or Brâhmanas should understand.

Religious life is the self-controlled, chaste practice of monks: avoiding harm, speaking gently, carefully receiving alms, and guarding mind, speech, body, and senses. It leads toward freedom from misery, while subtle actions acquire îryapathika Karman, experienced and destroyed within three moments.

Monks are defined by careful self-control: they avoid harming living creatures, practise chastity, austerities, and the three Guptis, and remain free from passions. Their disciplined conduct produces only subtle îryapathika Karman, immediately destroyed. They abstain from specially prepared food and harmful speech. Through long ascetic practice they attain Kêvala, then absolute perfection, enlightenment, deliverance, and final beatitude. By contrast, uncontrolled monks harm others; those who eat seeds, use cold water, and beg for a living are reborn repeatedly and do not end the Circle of Births.

Movable beings are one of the six classes of living beings. They arise from trees, creepers, grass, herbs, plants, water, and other bodies; feed on sap, humours, plants, and several kinds of bodies; and are subject to Karman. An uncontrolled creature may harm them to meet its wants, but injuring or killing them is sinful, while renouncing injury is vowed. When their life as movable beings ends, they may be reborn as movable or immovable beings.

Occult sciences include divination, signs, incantations, conjuring, oblations, martial arts, astrology, spells, and similar practices. Practised for worldly needs and pleasures, they are called wrong, unworthy, and mistaken, leading after death to Asuras and evildoers, then to disabilities including deafness and dumbness.

Perfection is an existent goal of the religious path. Monks obtain absolute perfection after attaining Kêvala; it accompanies enlightenment, deliverance, final beatitude, and the ending of all misery. It is not reached through unworthy, impure, harmful conduct, and has a place exclusively reserved for its attainments.
The mixed state concerns followers of the Sramanas, who practise righteousness partly and abstain from only some killing and sin; after death they are reborn as gods.

l: followers of the Sramanas, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: Followers of the Sramanas understand living and nonliving things, doctrine including Âsravas and Samvara, virtues, sins, Karman, bondage, and liberation. They practise vows, fasts, and self-purification, support Nirgrantha Sramanas, and confess sins. Although some cannot become monastics, they gradually conform through Pôsaha, limits, or fasting for death, and after perfection are reborn as gods.

Nirgrantha Sramanas are a group with a creed accepted by their followers, who provide food, clothing, medicines, and necessities. They are described as teaching or debating renunciation of injury to living beings; Gautama criticizes a teaching that renounces injury to movable beings while permitting it to immovable beings as noxious, misleading laymen, and voiding renunciation.

Philosophers comprise Kriyâvâda, Akriyâvâda, Agñânikavâda, and Vainayikavâda, who praise and publicize their doctrines; when challenged to hold burning coals, their refusal illustrates every creature’s aversion to pain.

l: three hundred and sixty-three philosophical schools, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: Three hundred and sixty-three philosophical schools, grouped under four vadas, teach final beatitude and deliverance while differing in intellect, will, character, opinions, taste, undertakings, and plans.

Kêvala knowledge is the highest, complete, unobstructed knowledge and faith. When full, it knows all things. Monks attain it while dying before absolute perfection and liberation; through meditation and teaching the whole Law, its possessors save themselves and others.

is_obtained_by monks [after attaining Kêvala] Enlightenment is attained by monks together with Kêvala, absolute perfection, and deliverance. It marks the end of misery and escape from further wandering.

is_obtained_by monks [after attaining Kêvala] Deliverance follows the attainment of Kêvala and absolute perfection by meritorious monks. It ends misery and frees beings from continued existence in Samsâra.

l: vessel full of burning coals, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: A vessel full of burning coals, carried with iron tongs, causes hand pain and tests philosophers’ willingness to endure it; their refusal supports aversion to pain.

l: iron pair of tongs, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: holds vessel full of burning coals [in the illustrative example] The iron pair of tongs is used to hold the vessel full of burning coals before it is offered to the philosophers. The philosophers are instructed not to use it themselves or extinguish the fire.

l: fourfold Circle of Births, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: The fourfold Circle of Births is an existent, beginningless and endless cycle marked by manifold pains. It unfolds through repeated cutting, piercing, birth, old age, death, conception, and regeneration. Violent beings, those bound by slaughter or acquisition of property, and others described as eating seeds, using cold water, or having intercourse with women remain repeatedly reborn. Beings shift between movable and immovable forms and bodies; wrong teachers cause ruin within it. Perfected beings end the cycle.

l: Third Lecture, Called Knowledge of Food, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: A lecture on food describes living beings’ birth, growth, nourishment, bodies, and Karman, concluding with care and circumspection regarding food.

Trees are living beings born, originated, and grown in earth. They consume earth, water, fire, wind, plants, and beings; arise because of Karman; and have manifold-coloured bodies. They arise from seeds at tops, roots, knots, or stems, while beings animating them feed on earth-liquid or tree sap.

is_a living beings [treated like trees in their modes of birth and growth] Creepers are treated like trees, including their origins, offshoots, roots, stems, branches, twigs, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds. Beings associated with creepers feed on their sap and consume various bodies.

is_a living beings [born in earth or water] Plants are described among the bodies in which beings are born, grow, and feed. Their roots and other parts, like those of trees, creepers, grass, and herbs, are associated with beings having manifold bodily qualities.

Earth-bodies are a class of living beings, including earth, gold, gravel, sand, stones, metals, minerals, and precious stones. Many living beings consume them; their associated beings have varied qualities. Resolving to meet wants through them is described as uncontrolled and sinful.

Water-bodies contain beings born and growing in water, including various aquatic plants and other movable creatures. Water-bodies may be produced by movable or immovable beings, by other water-bodies, or by wind, as in hoar-frost, snow, mist, hailstones, dew, and rain.

are_living_beings living beings [coming forth in animate or inanimate bodies] Beings come forth as fire-bodies in the manifold animate or inanimate bodies of movable or immovable creatures. The treatment of fire-bodies is continued in four paragraphs similar to those concerning water-bodies.

are_living_beings living beings [treated in the same way as fire-bodies] Wind-bodies are treated in the same way as fire-bodies and consist of four paragraphs. Their associated beings arise and are described through their relations to animate and inanimate bodies.

l: Fourth Lecture, Called Renunciation of Activity, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: A lecture explaining how uncontrolled activity leads the Self into sins and how a monk avoids and renounces them through teachings on living beings, sins, passions, and wrong belief.

argues sin [that sin requires sinful thoughts, speech, bodily functions, killing, an internal organ, consideration, or dreams] The opponent argues that there can be no sin without sinful thoughts, speech, bodily functions, killing, an internal organ, consideration of mental, verbal, and bodily activity, or seeing a dream. The opponent is answered that sin can exist despite the absence of these conditions.

assigns_as_reason six classes of living beings [for the existence of sin] The Âkârya answers the opponent by explaining that the six classes of living beings are the cause of sins and by using the examples of a murderer, a sentient being, and senseless beings. The Âkârya also teaches that one should avoid injuring or killing living beings because they feel pain as he does.
A sentient being with five senses and a developed internal organ may use six classes of living beings for wants; intending this makes it uncontrolled and sinful.
A senseless living being lacks reason, consciousness, intellect, mind, and speech, yet causes harm and is regarded as instrumental in bringing about sins.

is_a person with murderous intention [toward a householder, his son, the king, or his servant] A murderer who resolves to enter a house and kill a householder, his son, the king, or his servant is considered hostile and wrong day and night, whether sleeping or waking. His formed resolution is used to illustrate how intention makes him harmful even before the killing occurs.

l: five cardinal sins, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: includes wrong belief [as stated in the discourse's enumeration of sins and passions] The five cardinal sins include killing of living beings and are repeatedly connected with uncontrolled conduct and cruelty. A monk abstains from these sins.

l: mental, verbal, and bodily activity, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: is_a existent condition Mental, verbal, and bodily activity is not always consciously considered by the perpetrator of a sin. Nevertheless, failure to avoid and renounce harm can still result in sin even when such activity is not considered.

makes murderer [hostile and wrong day and night, sleeping or waking] Murderous intention is illustrated by the murderer who resolves to kill when an opportunity arises. An intention directed toward living beings generally is treated as harmful even when no particular being has been identified.
A monk practising chastity rejects heretical doctrines and bad conduct, follows the Ginas’ opinions, prioritizes final liberation over alms, and wanders until reaching liberation.

know_and_teach truth Beings are discussed in relation to whether there will be an end of those who know and teach the truth, whether all beings are alike, and whether they remain in perpetual bondage.
is_inaccessible_through alternatives [heretical alternatives] Truth cannot be reached through the stated heretical alternatives.
results_from alternatives [heretical alternatives] The heretical alternatives lead those who rely on them to error.
is_a existent entity Gîva exists, and the monk should not maintain that it does not exist.
is_a existent entity Agîva exists, and the monk should not maintain that it does not exist.
is_a existent entity Dharma exists, and the monk should not maintain that it does not exist.
is_a existent entity Adharma exists, and the monk should not maintain that it does not exist.
is_a existent state Bondage exists. The wrongly instructed Sramanas do not comprehend the soul's bondage through Karman.
is_a existent condition Âsrava exists.

l: stoppage of Âsrava, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: is_a existent condition The stoppage of Âsrava exists.
teach opinions The Ginas teach the opinions to which the monk should conform himself.

is_a Sramana [well-controlled and learned] Ârdraka defends Mahâvîra’s teaching and explains that a teacher may remain spiritually single while instructing many monks. He condemns harmful conduct, specially prepared food, slaughter, false doctrines, and the denial of guilt for injuring living beings.
Householders are said to perform the same acts as people who use cold water, eat seeds, and have intercourse with women; these acts do not distinguish Sramanas.
The Law is the supreme right path, teaching vows, control, compassion, harmless conduct, and pure livelihood through worthy teachers who live without deceit or secret sins.

avoids sin [through abstention from wicked deeds] Right conduct includes controlling oneself, guarding thoughts, words, and acts, avoiding injury, using virtuous speech, and abstaining from sinful food and behavior. Those who practise it are distinguished from those who lead blameable lives.

are_blameworthy wrong [when they are opposed to the right path] Doctrines are praised by their own teachers, and Sramanas and Brâhmanas blame one another while claiming truth for themselves. Ârdraka says that the wrong doctrines are blamed, not the personal qualities of those who hold them.

is_the_gain Sramanas [desired by a Sramana] Môksha is identified with the gain sought by a Sramana through the vow leading to Brahman. The teaching presents this gain as having a beginning but no end.

is_enjoined_by the Law Compassion toward all creatures is presented as a basis for avoiding sinful conduct and food specially prepared through slaughter. The Law that enjoins compassion is praised over a Law that permits slaughter.
Slaughter, caused by killing a fattened sheep for food, is condemned as against compassion; even annually killing one animal causes perdition and prevents becoming a Kêvalin.

l: Udaka, the son of Pêdhâla, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: Udaka, son of Pêdhâla, is a Nirgrantha follower of Pârsva of the Mêdârya Gôtra. Questioning Gautama about renouncing injury, he first defends a restricted view, then understands and respects Gautama’s teaching. In Gautama’s presence, he leaves the four-vow creed for Mahâvîra’s five great vows and Pratikramana.
Nâlandâ is a north-eastern suburb outside Râgagriha, containing hundreds of buildings and situated near Lêpa’s bathing-hall, Sêshadravyâ, and Hastiyâma park.

l: the creed which enjoins four vows, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: is_a creed The creed which enjoins four vows is the creed followed by Udaka before the conclusion of the unit. Udaka asks to pass from it to the creed which enjoins the five great vows and the Pratikramana.

l: the creed which enjoins the five great vows and the Pratikramana, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: is_a creed The creed which enjoins the five great vows and the Pratikramana is the creed to which Udaka changes in the presence of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra.

is_enjoined_by the creed which enjoins the five great vows and the Pratikramana Pratikramana is included in the creed to which Udaka asks to pass. He changes to the creed which enjoins the five great vows and the Pratikramana in the presence of the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra.

l: renunciation of injury to living beings, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: is_good good renunciation [when injury to the large class of movable beings is abandoned] Renunciation of injury to living beings is examined as a vow that may be limited to movable beings, limited by purpose or spatial boundaries, or extended to all beings. Gautama teaches that restricting it to one class cannot end injury altogether because beings change forms through rebirth.

l: death and rebirth, Sutrakritanga, Book II
s: is_governed_by Karman [in the next existence] Death ends a being’s current duration of life, after which the being is reborn as a movable or immovable being, within or beyond stated limits. The unit also discusses people who die after vows or fasting and then experience their Karman and receive either an evil or happy lot.

The records summarize the first eighteen lectures of the Uttaradhyayana Sutra, a teaching on liberation from Samsâra through disciplined ascetic conduct. Its central figures include Mahâvîra, Sudharman, Gautama, Kapila, King Nami, Harikêsa-Bala, Kitra, Brahmadatta, Bhrigu, Sañgaya, and other renouncers. The work begins by defining the obedient, truthful, restrained houseless monk and the hardships a wandering mendicant must patiently conquer. It presents rare human birth, instruction, belief, and self-control as requisites for ending Karman, while warning that carelessness, passion, greed, false asceticism, and attachment produce suffering, hell, and rebirth. It contrasts ignorant pursuit of pleasure with the wise acceptance of death, compassion, renunciation, penance, and careful almsgiving. Parables and teachings show that self-conquest exceeds worldly victory and that true religion rejects violence, possessions, sensuality, and merely external rites. Narrative examples then dramatize these lessons: Nami refuses restored kingship; Gautama abandons attachments; Harikêsa-Bala teaches that restraint and purity are the true sacrifice; Kitra reaches perfection while Brahmadatta falls into hell; and Bhrigu’s household and King Ishukâra renounce domestic life and attain perfection. The later lectures prescribe communal monastic discipline, perfect celibacy, and avoidance of careless or exploitative conduct, condemning the bad Sramana while praising the true monk. The sequence closes with King Sañgaya’s conversion after killing a deer, affirming that royal renunciation and righteous conduct lead beyond transient worldly ties toward heaven and perfection.
A translated first lecture presenting discipline and the conduct of a houseless monk.
is_about discipline The First Lecture explains discipline, obedience to a teacher, truthful speech, self-control, proper conduct, alms-gathering, and the keeping of the five vows.

Discipline concerns the houseless monk and is necessary for righteousness and avoiding rejection; one seeking liberation should eagerly pursue it. It becomes virtue through self-control, truthfulness, and right conduct, but egoism, delusion, carelessness, illness, and idleness make it impossible.

A monk is a houseless, poor wandering mendicant who has discarded worldly ties, property, former connections, attachment, hatred, pleasures, and desire for women. The central demand is disciplined self-control: he keeps the five vows, avoids untruth, sinful speech, deceit, killing, and injury in thought, word, and act; accepts only suitable alms for sustaining life; eats without daintiness; and follows the Law of ascetics strictly. He remains watchful and careful, guards his senses and celibacy, meditates, studies with zeal, acknowledges his teacher, and preaches the road of peace. His path requires enduring, learning, and conquering the twenty-two troubles without anger, attachment, forbidden conduct, or despair, while wandering without a fixed residence and bearing hardships. Human birth, hearing and believing the Law, and strenuous fulfillment of it lead him to restrain himself and shake off sinfulness. Outward ascetic marks alone do not ensure morality: an ignorant, egoistical, greedy, undisciplined, or loose-speaking monk is ill-behaved and may not reach Nirvâna. In contrast, humility, truthfulness, kindness, learning, austerities, and restraint make him worthy of instruction, superior to other monks, deep, fearless, and difficult to overcome. By conquering the will, casting aside fetters, annihilating Karman, and attaining self-discipline, Samvara, and contemplation, he reaches the highest place, liberation, or may become Siddha; restrained monks may also become gods of great power.
teacher instructs pupils in sacred text and conduct, gives orders and reprimands for their benefit, and is attended by people seeking deliverance; good pupils respect and obey him.

learns sacred text [according to tradition] The pupil should approach the teacher attentively, answer modestly, ask questions respectfully, accept instruction, avoid anger and lies, and carry out duties without needing repeated commands.
A well-behaved monk attentively obeys his teacher, observes proper conduct, responds when addressed, and follows rules.
An ill-behaved pupil is insubordinate and inattentive, difficult to instruct, may reject advice as hostility, and may be turned out.
is_preferred_to evil ways Virtue is what a brute turns away from when he takes to evil ways. The monk is urged to adhere to virtue for his own welfare.
supports welfare [one's own] Good conduct includes meekness, restraint in speech, truthful confession, respect for the teacher, patience, appropriate behavior, and avoidance of mean acts.
is_acquired_through discipline Righteousness is acquired through eagerness for discipline.

Liberation is the desired goal beyond the world: escape from existence, the Wheel of Births, and bondage. A son of the wise seeks it through discipline, conquering the will, watchfulness, faith, renunciation, the Law, penance, self-control, and absence of passion. It unfolds from desire and pursuit to choosing it over worldly objects, acting accordingly, and sustaining the body only to annihilate Karman.

Wise people value learning, patience, humility, and good conduct; monks must not offend them openly or secretly. They face death peacefully and without injury, weigh its kinds, and choose the better one taught in the Law of Compassion.
The self is difficult to subdue, yet self-control and penance subdue it, bringing happiness in this world and the next rather than punishment by others.

Self-control is a way of life and a means of subduing oneself, preferable to subjection through fetters and corporal punishment. Applied by one who has heard and believed the Law, it restrains the ascetic, shakes off sinfulness, and requires control of the senses. Saints surpass householders in it; with penance it may lead to high regions or liberation. It includes right exertion, tranquillity, protection by the five Samvaras, rejection of heretical doctrines, austerities, and self-restraint, as practised by Harikêsa, Gaya, and other kings.

Austerities are practised by a monk seeking freedom from greed after recognizing material insufficiency. They produce merit and spiritual power, subdue the self, and help keep the monk safe with meditation. Continual penance involves vows and enduring harsh conditions, visibly empowering Harikêsa.

has meaning A pupil who observes the rules of conduct may question the teacher about the sacred text, its meaning, or both. Worthy teachers may entrust such a pupil with extensive and weighty knowledge of the sacred texts.
Teacher’s kind or rough instruction is beneficial, producing patience and purity; intelligent monks welcome correction blissfully, while bad monks hate it.

Food and drink are alms for monks and ascetics, to be collected only when freely given under sanctioned rules and eaten moderately at the proper time. The ascetic must know the permitted quantity, avoid faults, wait apart, and accept food prepared for householders without attachment or disdain, including humble liquids and fare from lowly houses. In Harikêsa-Bala’s case, Brahmanas first refuse their prepared food, then seek forgiveness and offer boiled rice with condiments and other food and drink after his whole-month fast; he accepts it. Discipline in thought, word, and deed remains essential.
are_kept_by houseless monk [through austerities and meditation] A monk who gains knowledge, performs austerities, and meditates will keep the five vows.
Gods possess pleasures surpassing human pleasures; virtuous people attain their state, while renouncers expect godhood after leaving the body.

Men are of ten kinds. Those born into families with fields, houses, gold, cattle, slaves, and servants may possess friends and relations and be of good family, healthy, wise, noble, famous, and powerful. After enjoying unrivalled human pleasures, through pure religious merit acquired in a former life, they obtain true knowledge.

is_a eternal being [attained after shaking off the remnant of Karman] A being who perceives that the Four Requisites are difficult to obtain, applies himself to self-control, and shakes off the remnant of Karman through penances becomes an eternal Siddha.

Mahâvîra is a Venerable ascetic of Kâsyapa Gôtra and a teacher. Across lectures, he declares twenty-two troubles wandering monks must endure and conquer, describes death against one’s will as an ignorant pleasure-attached man’s cruel end, and teaches conditions for preserving chastity and fulfilling religious duties.

The twenty-two troubles are declared by the Kâsyapa and explained in due order. They span bodily hardship, unstable living conditions, abuse and refusal, illness and dirt, and contrasting experiences of respectful treatment, understanding, ignorance, and righteousness.

Wandering mendicant life is an ascetic monk’s life, entered by Bhrigu with his wife and sons, involving renunciation, penance, self-control, wandering, and alms. It brings severe hardships, requiring guarded passionlessness, and is chosen as a path toward liberation and ending misery.

Women are portrayed as naturally liked by men, called a slough and female demons, who entice and make sport of men. The lectures admonish monks not to desire or attach themselves to women, avoiding their company, conversation, appearance, sounds, and remembered pleasures.

l: places for sleep or rest, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: Places for sleep or rest should not be frequented by women, cattle, or eunuchs. Occupying such places may create doubt about a Nirgrantha's chastity or lead to sensual desire, remorse, rule-breaking, passion, illness, or abandonment of the faith.

is_committed_by young men [with sticks, canes, and whips] Harikêsa is mocked by the priests and assaulted by young men with sticks, canes, and whips while on his begging tour. Bhadrâ intervenes, Yakshas and Asuras protect him, and the Brahmanas later apologize for the injury and abuse.

Mendicancy requires Harikêsa to beg for food prepared for others, possess nothing, avoid cooking his food, and follow rules concerning walking, begging, speaking, easing nature, and receiving and keeping necessities.
A Sramana repeatedly suppresses delusion and controls himself, knowing and renouncing women; though roughly affected by externals, he must not hate them inwardly.

The Law is a noble, excellent, true teaching and enduring discipline, possessed by the wise and followed by the virtuous. It is difficult for living beings to hear, believe, fulfil, and practise, even when they have a human body, all five senses, or have been instructed; people may instead follow heretical teachers or embrace unrighteousness. A monk should meditate on it after corporal punishment, practise it with noble conduct, passionlessness, self-restraint, contentment, and attentiveness to chastity, continuing despite hardship, ignorance, and doubts about the Ginas. Its path includes penance, combating passions, non-injury, truth, righteousness, carefulness, patience, austerity, compassion, renunciation, and avoiding lying, taking what is not given, property, women, pride, and deceit. It teaches the consequences of virtue, sin, and transient worldly possessions: turning away leads the great sinner to hell and remorse at death, while following it leads toward gods, perfection, and freedom from rebirth. Nami becomes a Svayamsambuddha in the true Law; Brahmadatta knows it but does not follow it, while Kitra hears and practises it. It is a pond for spiritual purification, the only lasting safeguard at death, and an unchangeable, permanent, eternal Law proclaimed by the Ginas, through which the Siddhas reached perfection.
The Ginas are enlightened authorities who proclaim an eternal Law, teaching souls, sin’s consequences, and righteousness; Sañgaya and many kings adopt their faith.

Karman is the force produced by sinful thoughts and by living beings’ actions. It causes births in different forms, misery, separation, and a good or bad next existence; it follows its doer and must be borne alone. It drives the careless soul through Samsâra and burdens the ignorant sinner at death. The lectures present its overcoming through careful conduct, non-injury, penance, ascetic practice, right exertion, self-control, tranquillity, austerities, and renunciation. An ascetic sustains the body only to annihilate Karman, while Harikêsa treats it as fuel for an inner sacrifice and Nami likens it to a foe’s mail pierced by penance. As Karman ceases, beings may attain a pure state and birth as men; when its remnant is shaken off, they may become an eternal Siddha.

is_represented_by human life [in the merchants’ parable] Capital represents human life. Bringing back the capital represents rebirth as a man, while increasing it represents attaining the state of gods.

is_a ritual element [tended by Brahmanas] The Brahmanas ask where the monks’ fire and fireplace are and what oblations they offer. Harikêsa answers that penance is his fire, life is his fireplace, and Karman is its fuel.

is_used_for external purity [in Brahmanical ritual] The Brahmanas use water morning and evening in pursuit of external purity. Harikêsa teaches that such external purity is not the right kind and that true purification comes through the Law, celibacy, and removal of hatred.

is_a teaching The Discourse is heard by Sudharman from the Venerable Mahâvîra and concerns the enumeration and explanation of the twenty-two troubles. It teaches how a monk should bear and conquer each trouble.

is_a things of paramount value [difficult to obtain here by a living being] The Four Requisites are human birth, instruction in the Law, belief in it, and energy in self-control. They are difficult for a living being to obtain.

Human birth is a difficult, paramount and rare chance for a living being, attained in due time through cessation of Karman. Even after becoming human, becoming an Ârya, possessing five senses, receiving, believing, and practising the best Law remain rare.

l: instruction in the Law, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: is_a requisite [of paramount value and difficult to obtain] Instruction in the Law is difficult to obtain even for those born with a human body. Hearing it enables beings to do penances, combat their passions, and abstain from killing living beings.

l: belief in the Law, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: is_a requisite [of paramount value and difficult to obtain] Belief in the Law is difficult to obtain even after hearing it, because many who are shown the right way stray from it.

is_a requisite [of paramount value and difficult to obtain] Energy in self-control is difficult to fulfill strenuously, even for those who have heard and believed in the Law. Many who approve of the religion do not adopt it.

Living beings move through Samsâra according to their actions: born in different families, castes, and non-human forms, suffering pains and recurring births without disgust, like warriors in life’s battle. They may become gods, hells, Asuras, Kshattriyas, Kandâlas, Bukkasas, worms, moths, Kunthu, or ants. By cessation of Karman, they may in due time be born as men and reach a pure state. They people the world, moving or unmoving, and should not be injured by a monk in thought, word, or act.

Samsâra is the endless, unstable Wheel of Births: a condition of recurring births inhabited by living beings and full of misery. Beings become many forms, from gods and hell-beings to worms and ants, yet are not disgusted with its misery. Personal actions, good and bad Karman, attachment to bodies and pleasures, sins, wrong actions, and carelessness drive and keep them moving through it, unable to escape their effects. Ignorant and sinful men suffer and wander long within it. Pious ascetics cross it, while a sage who uses spiritual weapons, faith, penance, self-control, patience, zeal, carefulness, content, and truth, defeats and gets rid of Samsâra.
Fourth Lecture says people cannot escape actions’ effects in this life and the next, regardless of relatives’ aid or motives.
Asuras are a world where undisciplined seekers of pleasures are reborn, assault young men in hideous aerial shapes, then err long in Samsâra after rising.
Penances help beings shake off Karman; ascetics with the Four Requisites can reach the highest Nirvâna.
ensnare men adhering to wrong principles Passions ensnare people and subject them to hatred, love, and other harmful influences.

l: killing of living beings, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: The preceptors who proclaimed the Law of ascetics taught that killing of living beings should not be permitted or consented to. Avoiding it may deliver a person from all misery.
The highest Nirvâna is reached by the pure soul, firmly standing in the Law, like a fire fed with ghee.

Yakshas are virtuous beings who inhabit heaven and heavenly regions one above another, shining like great luminaries. They enjoy divine pleasures in the upper Kalpa heavens, change form at will, and remain there according to merit. At life’s end they descend and are born as men; they also pay homage to Nirgrantha.

surpass human pleasures [by a thousand times and more] Divine pleasures surpass human pleasures a thousand times and more. Their superiority shows the smallness of the pleasures available in human life.

l: the upper Kalpa heavens, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: The upper Kalpa heavens are regions where Yakshas live for many centuries of former years. There they enjoy divine pleasures and change their form at will.

is_obtained_by men [through pure religious merit acquired in a former life] True knowledge is obtained by a man through pure religious merit acquired in a former life, after he has enjoyed the unrivalled pleasures of human life at their proper time.
is_about Impurity The Fourth Lecture teaches about impurity, carelessness, the consequences of actions, and the discipline required for liberation.
Impurity is associated with wrong principles, passions, delusion, deceit, greed, and heretics.

exposes_to old age [when life is not prolonged] Carelessness leaves people without protection and unable to benefit from having seen the right way. A person should never be careless because life is limited and the body is weak.

Human life is finite, fleeting, and precarious: it cannot be prolonged indefinitely and soon ends like a fallow leaf or dew-drop. Compared to capital entrusted to a merchant, it can be restored or increased through virtue, but lost through sin; its brevity urges conquering the will, wiping off sins, and practising the Law.
does_not_protect carelessness [in this world and the next] Wealth acquired through evil deeds will be lost, and wealth cannot protect a careless person in this world or the next.
holds_captive men adhering to wrong principles A monk should cast aside hatred and should not sink through it. A monk who does not love even those who love him will be freed from hatred.
Enlightenment is described as the stake a monk seeks after first taking care of his life and then annihilating his sins.
is_conquered_by monk Conquering the will leads to liberation. Delaying victory over the will is dangerous because human life may end before it is achieved.

Pleasures are impermanent sensual enjoyments that resemble poison, thorns, and a venomous snake. Attachment causes anger, pain, repeated error, downfall, and continued worldly existence, while their happiness is slight and suffering prolonged. A person who does not renounce them misses the soul’s true end; one who renounces them may attain a godly state. Nami first enjoys and then abandons pleasures before enlightenment, whereas Brahmadatta continues longing for them despite knowing the Law. Ultimately, abandoning pleasures removes an obstacle to liberation.
Delusion is to be kept out of mind and repeatedly suppressed because it weakens intellect and blocks one’s path; King Nami ends its influence and remembers his former birth.
External things weaken intellect and allure many; monks may be affected roughly but should not hate them mentally.
Heretics are impure and vain, ruled by love, hate, and passions; they should desire virtues until life’s end.
Good actions are desired throughout life, bear fruit for people, bring wealth and prosperity, and are practiced to avoid regret after death.

l: death against one's will, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: Death against one’s will is repeatedly experienced by ignorant men when fear, transgression of the Law, and unrighteousness bring a fool’s death.

l: death with one's will, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: Death with one's will is the once-at-best death of wise men, reached through one of three methods when the time for quitting the body has come.
Ignorant men are attached to pleasures and amusements, commit cruel actions and sin, suffer disease and fear hell, then repent at death and undergo it against their will.
Pleasures cause grief through attachment; weak men struggle to abandon them, while monks should choose discipline or risk Asura birth.

Sin is accumulated by ignorant people through overbearing, desirous, cruel, deceitful, and undisciplined conduct. A monk abstains from it by protecting the soul, subduing the senses, and living without ties. Avoiding indulgence, harm, greed, deceit, improper conduct, and dependence makes one pious and victorious in this world and the next.

Hell is a place and state of misery where fools and great sinners suffer violently. It awaits those who commit cruel, unrighteous deeds or pursue pleasures after turning from the Law. Even mendicants cannot escape; Brahmadatta reaches it after rejecting Kitra’s counsel and enjoying sensual pleasures.

The virtuous man is self-controlled and nonviolent, subduing his senses and turning from unrighteousness to follow the true Law. He does not tremble at death; through discipline, he attains heavenly regions or liberation and is born as a god.

Householders possess morality of various character; some surpass monks in self-control. Faithful householders should practise rules of conduct and observe the Pôsaha fast in both fortnights. Living piously under discipline, quitting flesh and bones, they may share Yakshas and obtain liberation through self-control, penance, and absence of passion. They prepare food for their own consumption, while monks do not pursue them for earthly gain.
